data.title: English Prepositions
data.description: Choose the correct sentence for each preposition. Includes core prepositions plus B2+ multi-word and formal prepositions.

sections.title: in
sections.summary: IN is used for enclosed spaces, months/years, and general periods.
sections.explain: Use IN for something inside boundaries (in the box, in London) and for longer time periods (in 2026, in June).

words.word: The report will be ready in June.
The report will be ready on June.
The report will be ready at June.

sections.title: on
sections.summary: ON is used for surfaces and specific days/dates.
sections.explain: Use ON for contact with a surface (on the table) and for days/dates (on Monday, on 12 March).

words.word: We met on Monday to finalise the budget.
We met in Monday to finalise the budget.
We met at Monday to finalise the budget.

sections.title: at
sections.summary: AT is used for precise times and specific points/locations.
sections.explain: Use AT for clock times (at 7:30) and for a specific point (at the entrance, at the corner).

words.word: Let’s meet at 7:30 outside the station.
Let’s meet on 7:30 outside the station.
Let’s meet in 7:30 outside the station.

sections.title: by
sections.summary: BY often means 'no later than' or shows method/means.
sections.explain: Use BY for deadlines (by Friday) and for method (by email, by train). It does not mean 'until' in duration.

words.word: Please send the signed contract by Friday.
Please send the signed contract until Friday.
Please send the signed contract since Friday.

sections.title: until
sections.summary: UNTIL marks the end point of a continuing situation.
sections.explain: Use UNTIL to show something continues up to a time and then stops/changes (stay until 6).

words.word: I’ll be in the office until 6, then I’m heading home.
I’ll be in the office by 6, then I’m heading home.
I’ll be in the office for 6, then I’m heading home.

sections.title: for
sections.summary: FOR is used for duration and purpose/benefit.
sections.explain: Use FOR with a period of time (for two weeks) and to indicate purpose/benefit (for you).

words.word: They lived in Berlin for two years before moving back.
They lived in Berlin since two years before moving back.
They lived in Berlin during two years before moving back.

sections.title: since
sections.summary: SINCE is used from a starting point up to now/then.
sections.explain: Use SINCE with a starting time (since 2019) to show a situation continues to the present or to a later reference point.

words.word: I’ve worked remotely since 2020.
I’ve worked remotely for 2020.
I’ve worked remotely during 2020.

sections.title: during
sections.summary: DURING means 'at some point in the period'.
sections.explain: Use DURING for something happening within a period (during the meeting, during the night).

words.word: Please keep your phone on silent during the presentation.
Please keep your phone on silent for the presentation.
Please keep your phone on silent since the presentation.

sections.title: between
sections.summary: BETWEEN is for two items (or clear endpoints).
sections.explain: Use BETWEEN for two people/things, or for ranges with two endpoints (between 3 and 5).

words.word: The agreement is between the supplier and the distributor.
The agreement is among the supplier and the distributor.
The agreement is within the supplier and the distributor.

sections.title: among
sections.summary: AMONG is for three or more items as a group.
sections.explain: Use AMONG when something is distributed or shared within a group of three or more.

words.word: The bonus will be shared among the five team members.
The bonus will be shared between the five team members.
The bonus will be shared across of the five team members.

sections.title: into
sections.summary: INTO suggests movement to the inside of something.
sections.explain: Use INTO when something moves from outside to inside (walk into the room).

words.word: She walked into the room without knocking.
She walked in the room without knocking.
She walked onto the room without knocking.

sections.title: onto
sections.summary: ONTO suggests movement to a surface.
sections.explain: Use ONTO when something moves to a surface (put it onto the table).

words.word: He placed the documents onto the desk and sat down.
He placed the documents into the desk and sat down.
He placed the documents at the desk and sat down.

sections.title: within
sections.summary: WITHIN means 'inside a limit' (time/space/rules).
sections.explain: Use WITHIN for limits and deadlines measured from now/then (within 24 hours) and boundaries (within the site).

words.word: You must submit the form within 24 hours of receiving the link.
You must submit the form by 24 hours of receiving the link.
You must submit the form until 24 hours of receiving the link.

sections.title: throughout
sections.summary: THROUGHOUT means 'from start to finish' of a whole period/place.
sections.explain: Use THROUGHOUT when something applies continuously across an entire period or area (throughout the year/country).

words.word: The policy remained in force throughout the year.
The policy remained in force during the year (meaning only at some times).
The policy remained in force by the year.

sections.title: over
sections.summary: OVER can mean 'more than' or 'covering a period'.
sections.explain: Use OVER for duration/coverage (over the next few weeks) and for 'more than' (over £100).

words.word: Sales increased steadily over the next three months.
Sales increased steadily in the next three months.
Sales increased steadily at the next three months.

sections.title: under
sections.summary: UNDER can mean 'beneath' or 'subject to'.
sections.explain: Use UNDER for physical position and for rules/authority (under the contract, under pressure).

words.word: Under the current contract, refunds are limited.
Below the current contract, refunds are limited.
Between the current contract, refunds are limited.

sections.title: above
sections.summary: ABOVE is often used in formal writing to refer to earlier text or higher values.
sections.explain: Use ABOVE to refer to something earlier in a document (as stated above) or higher levels/values.

words.word: As stated above, all claims must include evidence.
As stated over, all claims must include evidence.
As stated across, all claims must include evidence.

sections.title: below
sections.summary: BELOW is used for lower position or later text.
sections.explain: Use BELOW for lower position, lower values, or later text (see below).

words.word: Please see the detailed breakdown below.
Please see the detailed breakdown under.
Please see the detailed breakdown beneath of.

sections.title: beneath
sections.summary: BENEATH is like 'under' but more formal/literary.
sections.explain: Use BENEATH for something lower in position, often in more formal or descriptive writing.

words.word: The safe was hidden beneath the floorboards.
The safe was hidden below the floorboards (could be okay, but less exact for contact/cover).
The safe was hidden under of the floorboards.

sections.title: towards
sections.summary: TOWARDS indicates direction or attitude.
sections.explain: Use TOWARDS for movement in a direction (towards the exit) or attitude (towards change).

words.word: She moved towards the door as the meeting ended.
She moved until the door as the meeting ended.
She moved within the door as the meeting ended.

sections.title: through
sections.summary: THROUGH suggests passing from one side to the other.
sections.explain: Use THROUGH for movement across an enclosed space or process (through the tunnel; through negotiations).

words.word: We got through security faster than expected.
We got across security faster than expected.
We got along security faster than expected.

sections.title: across
sections.summary: ACROSS means from one side to the other (often on a surface/area).
sections.explain: Use ACROSS for movement from one side to another across an area (across the road/field).

words.word: He ran across the road without looking.
He ran through the road without looking.
He ran over the road without looking.

sections.title: along
sections.summary: ALONG suggests movement following a line (road/river).
sections.explain: Use ALONG when you move next to and following something long and thin (along the river, along the street).

words.word: We walked along the river to avoid traffic.
We walked across the river to avoid traffic.
We walked into the river to avoid traffic.

sections.title: via
sections.summary: VIA means 'through' or 'by way of' (route/method).
sections.explain: Use VIA to indicate a route or method, especially in formal contexts (via email, via Paris).

words.word: Please submit your request via the online portal.
Please submit your request by the online portal.
Please submit your request with the online portal.

sections.title: per
sections.summary: PER means 'for each' (formal).
sections.explain: Use PER in measurements and rates (per hour, per person). It’s more formal than 'a/an' or 'each'.

words.word: The service costs £10 per user per month.
The service costs £10 by user per month.
The service costs £10 for user per month.

sections.title: despite
sections.summary: DESPITE is used to show contrast.
sections.explain: Use DESPITE + noun/gerund to show something happened even though there was an obstacle.

words.word: Despite the delays, the project launched on time.
Despite of the delays, the project launched on time.
Although the delays, the project launched on time.

sections.title: in spite of
sections.summary: IN SPITE OF is like DESPITE but slightly longer/more emphatic.
sections.explain: Use IN SPITE OF + noun/gerund to show strong contrast.

words.word: In spite of the criticism, she stuck to her plan.
In spite the criticism, she stuck to her plan.
In spite of she was criticised, she stuck to her plan.

sections.title: because of
sections.summary: BECAUSE OF gives a reason (followed by a noun phrase).
sections.explain: Use BECAUSE OF + noun phrase. Use BECAUSE + clause.

words.word: The flight was cancelled because of bad weather.
The flight was cancelled because bad weather.
The flight was cancelled because of it was raining.

sections.title: owing to
sections.summary: OWING TO is a formal alternative to 'because of'.
sections.explain: Use OWING TO + noun phrase in formal writing (owing to circumstances).

words.word: Owing to staffing shortages, the office will close early.
Owing to we are short-staffed, the office will close early.
Owing for staffing shortages, the office will close early.

sections.title: due to
sections.summary: DUE TO is often used to mean 'caused by' (formal).
sections.explain: In careful usage, DUE TO links to a noun (The delay was due to...). Many speakers also use it like 'because of'.

words.word: The delay was due to a technical fault.
The delay was due to the train was late.
The delay was owing that a technical fault.

sections.title: according to
sections.summary: ACCORDING TO introduces a source.
sections.explain: Use ACCORDING TO to reference information from a person/document/source.

words.word: According to the forecast, the storm will arrive tonight.
According the forecast, the storm will arrive tonight.
Depending to the forecast, the storm will arrive tonight.

sections.title: regardless of
sections.summary: REGARDLESS OF means 'it doesn’t matter'.
sections.explain: Use REGARDLESS OF + noun/gerund to show something is true even if conditions change.

words.word: We will proceed regardless of the outcome.
We will proceed regardless the outcome.
We will proceed despite of the outcome.

sections.title: instead of
sections.summary: INSTEAD OF means 'as a replacement'.
sections.explain: Use INSTEAD OF + noun/gerund to show substitution.

words.word: He took the train instead of driving.
He took the train instead driving.
He took the train rather than of driving.

sections.title: rather than
sections.summary: RATHER THAN expresses preference/contrast.
sections.explain: Use RATHER THAN to contrast two options (do X rather than Y).

words.word: I’d email the client rather than call them without warning.
I’d email the client rather than to call them without warning.
I’d email the client instead than call them without warning.

sections.title: apart from
sections.summary: APART FROM can mean 'except for' or 'in addition to' (context matters).
sections.explain: Use APART FROM to exclude something (apart from one detail) or add something (apart from that, ...).

words.word: Apart from one minor typo, the proposal is excellent.
Apart of one minor typo, the proposal is excellent.
Apart from the proposal is excellent, one minor typo.

sections.title: aside from
sections.summary: ASIDE FROM is similar to 'apart from' (except for).
sections.explain: Use ASIDE FROM + noun phrase to mean 'except for'.

words.word: Aside from the cost, the solution is ideal.
Aside the cost, the solution is ideal.
Aside from it is expensive, the solution is ideal.

sections.title: as of
sections.summary: AS OF means 'from that date/time'.
sections.explain: Use AS OF to indicate an official starting point (as of 1 April, new rules apply).

words.word: As of 1 April, the company will adopt a new policy.
As from 1 April, the company will adopt a new policy.
As at 1 April, the company will adopt a new policy.

sections.title: as per
sections.summary: AS PER means 'according to' (formal/business).
sections.explain: Use AS PER in formal/business English to refer to instructions or a previous agreement.

words.word: As per your email, we have updated the schedule.
As per you emailed, we have updated the schedule.
As by your email, we have updated the schedule.

sections.title: prior to
sections.summary: PRIOR TO is a formal alternative to 'before'.
sections.explain: Use PRIOR TO + noun/gerund in formal writing (prior to departure).

words.word: Prior to departure, please double-check your documents.
Prior of departure, please double-check your documents.
Prior to you depart, please double-check your documents.

sections.title: subsequent to
sections.summary: SUBSEQUENT TO is a formal alternative to 'after'.
sections.explain: Use SUBSEQUENT TO + noun/gerund in formal contexts (subsequent to the meeting).

words.word: Subsequent to the meeting, the minutes were circulated.
Subsequent the meeting, the minutes were circulated.
Subsequent to we met, the minutes were circulated.

sections.title: in addition to
sections.summary: IN ADDITION TO means 'as well as' (followed by a noun/gerund).
sections.explain: Use IN ADDITION TO + noun/gerund, not a full clause.

words.word: In addition to reviewing the draft, she proposed new examples.
In addition to she reviewed the draft, she proposed new examples.
In addition with reviewing the draft, she proposed new examples.

sections.title: in terms of
sections.summary: IN TERMS OF sets the aspect/criteria you are discussing.
sections.explain: Use IN TERMS OF to specify the perspective (in terms of cost, speed, risk). Avoid overusing it.

words.word: In terms of reliability, this model performs best.
In term of reliability, this model performs best.
On terms of reliability, this model performs best.

sections.title: with regard to
sections.summary: WITH REGARD TO means 'concerning' (formal).
sections.explain: Use WITH REGARD TO to introduce the topic, often in business writing.

words.word: With regard to your complaint, we are investigating the issue.
With regards to your complaint, we are investigating the issue.
With regard of your complaint, we are investigating the issue.

sections.title: in relation to
sections.summary: IN RELATION TO means 'concerning' or 'compared with'.
sections.explain: Use IN RELATION TO for connections between topics or for comparison in formal language.

words.word: In relation to last quarter, profits have improved.
In relation with last quarter, profits have improved.
In relation last quarter, profits have improved.

sections.title: in respect of
sections.summary: IN RESPECT OF is very formal and means 'regarding'.
sections.explain: Use IN RESPECT OF in legal/official contexts to refer to a specific matter.

words.word: Payment is due in respect of services provided in December.
Payment is due with respect of services provided in December.
Payment is due in respect to services provided in December.

sections.title: with respect to
sections.summary: WITH RESPECT TO means 'regarding' (formal/neutral).
sections.explain: Use WITH RESPECT TO to introduce a topic in formal English; it is common in technical writing.

words.word: With respect to safety, the new procedure reduces risk.
With respect of safety, the new procedure reduces risk.
With respects to safety, the new procedure reduces risk.

sections.title: in accordance with
sections.summary: IN ACCORDANCE WITH means 'following/complying with'.
sections.explain: Use IN ACCORDANCE WITH to state that something follows rules, law, or instructions.

words.word: The data was processed in accordance with company policy.
The data was processed in accordance to company policy.
The data was processed in accordance of company policy.

sections.title: in line with
sections.summary: IN LINE WITH means 'consistent with'.
sections.explain: Use IN LINE WITH when something matches a standard, expectation, or trend.

words.word: The new pricing is in line with market rates.
The new pricing is on line with market rates.
The new pricing is in line to market rates.

sections.title: on behalf of
sections.summary: ON BEHALF OF means 'representing' or 'for'.
sections.explain: Use ON BEHALF OF when someone acts as a representative (on behalf of the team/company).

words.word: I’m writing on behalf of the recruitment team.
I’m writing in behalf of the recruitment team.
I’m writing on behalf the recruitment team.

sections.title: in favour of
sections.summary: IN FAVOUR OF means supporting/choosing one option.
sections.explain: Use IN FAVOUR OF to show preference or support (vote in favour of; decide in favour of).

words.word: They voted in favour of the proposed merger.
They voted on favour of the proposed merger.
They voted in favour for the proposed merger.

sections.title: in light of
sections.summary: IN LIGHT OF means 'considering new information'.
sections.explain: Use IN LIGHT OF to introduce a reason based on recent facts (in light of recent events...).

words.word: In light of recent findings, we will revise the guidelines.
In the light for recent findings, we will revise the guidelines.
On light of recent findings, we will revise the guidelines.

sections.title: by means of
sections.summary: BY MEANS OF means 'using' (formal).
sections.explain: Use BY MEANS OF to describe the method used to achieve something, often in formal writing.

words.word: The device is activated by means of a secure code.
The device is activated by means to a secure code.
The device is activated with means of a secure code.

sections.title: by virtue of
sections.summary: BY VIRTUE OF means 'because of' (formal, often legal).
sections.explain: Use BY VIRTUE OF to explain why something is true due to a quality/status/law.

words.word: By virtue of her role, she has access to confidential data.
By virtue to her role, she has access to confidential data.
By virtue of she is a manager, she has access to confidential data.

sections.title: in the event of
sections.summary: IN THE EVENT OF means 'if something happens' (formal).
sections.explain: Use IN THE EVENT OF + noun/gerund, common in instructions and warnings.

words.word: In the event of a fire, use the stairs and do not use the lift.
In the event a fire, use the stairs and do not use the lift.
In the event of it catches fire, use the stairs and do not use the lift.

sections.title: in case of
sections.summary: IN CASE OF is used for precautions about possible events.
sections.explain: Use IN CASE OF + noun for warnings/instructions (in case of emergency). It differs from 'in case' + clause.

words.word: Keep this receipt in case of any issues with the product.
Keep this receipt in case any issues with the product.
Keep this receipt in case of you have issues with the product.

sections.title: in lieu of
sections.summary: IN LIEU OF means 'instead of' (formal).
sections.explain: Use IN LIEU OF + noun/gerund in formal contexts (in lieu of payment; in lieu of a refund).

words.word: We offered store credit in lieu of a cash refund.
We offered store credit in lieu for a cash refund.
We offered store credit in place of to a cash refund.

sections.title: in return for
sections.summary: IN RETURN FOR shows exchange/compensation.
sections.explain: Use IN RETURN FOR to indicate what you receive as a result of giving something.

words.word: He volunteered extra hours in return for time off later.
He volunteered extra hours in return to time off later.
He volunteered extra hours in exchange of time off later.

sections.title: for the sake of
sections.summary: FOR THE SAKE OF means 'to achieve/preserve something'.
sections.explain: Use FOR THE SAKE OF + noun/gerund to show purpose, often involving a compromise.

words.word: For the sake of clarity, let’s define the terms first.
For sake of clarity, let’s define the terms first.
For the sake to clarity, let’s define the terms first.

sections.title: with a view to
sections.summary: WITH A VIEW TO means 'in order to' (followed by a noun/gerund).
sections.explain: Use WITH A VIEW TO + noun/gerund (with a view to improving...). It does not take an infinitive directly.

words.word: They redesigned the workflow with a view to reducing errors.
They redesigned the workflow with a view to reduce errors.
They redesigned the workflow for a view to reducing errors.

sections.title: notwithstanding
sections.summary: NOTWITHSTANDING means 'despite' (very formal).
sections.explain: Use NOTWITHSTANDING + noun phrase to mean 'in spite of'. Common in legal/official writing.

words.word: Notwithstanding the risks, they approved the investment.
Notwithstanding of the risks, they approved the investment.
Notwithstanding they were aware of the risks, they approved the investment.
